analysis.one_liner: Conditions federal backing of manufactured home community loans on minimum tenant protections.
analysis.headline: The bill never left the House Financial Services Committee; it was introduced with 9 Democratic supporters and received no hearing or vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Owners of manufactured home communities could only get federally backed loans — government-insured loans or loans bought by Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac — if they gave residents protections in their leases: one-year renewable leases, 60-day notice of rent increases with written justification, a grace period for rent, the right to sell their home in place, notice and a negotiation window before the community is sold or closed, and penalties for violations. The bill never received a hearing or vote in the House Financial Services Committee and died when the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Residents of manufactured home communities — mostly lower-income households who own their home but rent the land under it — gain protection from sudden rent increases, lease non-renewals, and eviction-forced home sales. The bill reaches them through financing: any owner wanting a HUD-insured loan or a loan purchased by Fannie Mae or Freddie Mac would have to adopt the protections across every community it owns.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Residents who own their home but rent the lot

how_it_helps.text: Borrowers seeking federal loan backing must certify that every community they or an affiliate own includes minimum tenant protections in their leases, covering leases, notice, grace periods, sale rights, and termination reasons.

Rent increases require at least 60 days written notice with a written justification of operating costs, and each increase over 5 percent of prior rent requires an extra 30 days notice per additional 2.5 percent increase.

Tenants gain the right to sell their home in place without relocating it, to keep a 'For Sale' sign up, to sublease to a buyer, and to receive 60-day notice — including price and terms — before the community is sold, with a 60-day window during which the owner must negotiate in good faith if tenants want to buy the community.

Owners who willfully violate the protections can be barred from future federally backed financing for at least two years, and must pay tenants specified damages, such as six months rent for wrongful termination or the increased rent repaid with 25 percent interest for improper increases.

Any pricing discounts offered under the covered loan programs must reward protections stronger than the bill's minimums, and a new commission — required to include a current manufactured housing resident — must propose additional standards within a year.

analysis.who_pays: Owners and investors of manufactured home communities bear the cost: they must adopt the lease protections to keep access to HUD-insured loans and Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac purchases, and face penalties and temporary loss of federal financing access if they violate them.

drawbacks.text: The requirements only apply to owners seeking HUD insurance or Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac purchases, so owners financing with private capital escape the protections entirely.

A good-faith objection: conditioning loan eligibility on tenant protections could make financing for community construction, rehabilitation, or purchase somewhat scarcer or more expensive, a cost that could ultimately fall partly on residents if financing dries up.
The bill authorizes no new funding, so oversight and enforcement by HUD and the Federal Housing Finance Agency would have to come from existing budgets.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the residents of these communities — who typically own a depreciating home but rent the pad under it and have little leverage against investor owners — the protections address the core vulnerabilities: sudden rent hikes, non-renewal, and forced relocation to sell. The costs fall mainly on owners' financing terms, and the design limits the burden by attaching conditions only to federal loan programs rather than regulating all communities directly. The main real weakness is the financing-only reach and its enforcement burden on existing agency budgets.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Financial Services Committee, which never acted on it, so it died when the 118th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Brittany Pettersen introduced the Manufactured Housing Tenant's Bill of Rights Act of 2023 on July 11, 2023, with Reps. Bonamici and Omar as original cosponsors.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services the same day; no further action was ever taken on it.
The bill finished with 8 cosponsors, all Democrats.
When the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, the bill had received no hearing, no markup, and no floor vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Owners and investors of manufactured home communities are better off: they keep access to federally backed financing without having to accept lease protections, and residents remain exposed to the rent increases and lease terminations the bill would have restricted.

against.name: House Financial Services Committee
against.role: Committee of referral (chaired by Rep. Patrick McHenry, R-NC)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never scheduled a hearing or markup, leaving it to die at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's sponsor and all 8 cosponsors were Democrats, and the Republican-controlled Financial Services Committee took no action; there were no votes to measure broader support.

industries.industry: Manufactured home community owners and investors
industries.note: The bill conditions access to HUD-insured loans and Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac purchases on adopting lease protections, and imposes penalties including temporary exclusion from federal financing. Investor owners profit from raising lot rents and controlling whether residents can sell their homes, so their financial interest in this bill ran directly against residents' interests.

industries.industry: Mortgage lenders and brokers serving the sector
industries.note: Lenders making community loans would face new certification and documentation requirements and, for noncompliant borrowers, reduced eligibility, but lenders serving compliant owners would keep their deal flow under the covered programs.
